By default, this API server endpoint is public to the internet, and access to the API server is secured using a combination of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) along with native Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Enabling private access to the Kubernetes API server ensures that all communication between your nodes and the API server stays within your VPC. You can limit the IP addresses that have access to your API server from the internet, or you can completely disallow internet access to the API server\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/controlreference/eks-rules.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I securely access the Amazon EKS cluster API server endpoint from within a VPC or peered VPC?\",\"context\":\"#### Use the AWS Management Console to modify your cluster API server endpoint access\\n\\n1. Open the [Amazon EKS console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/eks/home#/clusters).\\n2. Select the name of the cluster to display your cluster information.\\n3. Open the **Networking** tab, and then choose **Update**.\\n4. Choose whether to Turn on or off private access for your cluster's Kubernetes API server endpoint. If you turn on private access, then Kubernetes API requests that originate from within your cluster's VPC use the private VPC endpoint. To turn off public access, you must first turn on private access.\\n5. Choose whether to turn on or off public access for your cluster's Kubernetes API server endpoint. If you turn off public access, then your cluster's Kubernetes API server can only receive requests from within the cluster VPC.\\n6. Choose **Update**\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/eks-cluster-api-secure-access-within-vpc\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Remediating exposures for Amazon EKS clusters\",\"context\":\"### The Amazon EKS cluster allows public access\\n\\nThe Amazon EKS cluster endpoint is the endpoint that you use to communicate with your cluster\u2019s Kubernetes API server.\\nBy default, this endpoint is public to the internet.\\nPublic endpoints increase your attack surface area and the risk of unauthorized access to your Kubernetes API server, potentially allowing attackers to access or modify cluster resources or access sensitive data.\\nFollowing security best practices, restrict access to your Amazon EKS cluster endpoint to only necessary IP ranges.\\n\\n###### Remediation\\n\\nTake one or more of the following actions to address this exposure:\\n\\n###### Modify endpoint access\\n\\nIn the exposure finding, open the resource. This opens the affected Amazon EKS cluster. You can configure your cluster to use private access, public access, or both.\\n\\nWith private access, Kubernetes API requests that originate within your cluster\u2019s VPC use the private VPC endpoint. With public access, Kubernetes API requests that originate from outside your cluster\u2019s VPC use the public endpoint.\\n\\n###### Modify or remove public access to the cluster\\n\\nTo modify endpoint access for an existing cluster, see Modifying cluster endpoint access in the *Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service User Guide*.\\nImplement more restrictive rules based on specific IP ranges or security groups.\\nIf limited public access is necessary, restrict access to specific CIDR block ranges or use prefix lists\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/exposure-eks-cluster.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Running Verify Aws Claim"}

This new benchmark is optimized to help you accurately assess the security configuration of Amazon EKS clusters, including security assessments for nodes to help meet security and compliance requirements.\\\\n\\\\nSecurity is a critical consideration when configuring and maintaining Kubernetes clusters and applications. Amazon EKS provides secure, managed Kubernetes clusters by default, but you still need to ensure that you configure the nodes and applications securely and meet your security and compliance requirements. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark provides good practice guidance on security configurations for unmanaged Kubernetes clusters where you typically manage the Kubernetes cluster control plane and nodes. The benchmark does not sufficiently cover the different configuration mechanisms used by Amazon EKS. This means that if you\u2019re using the CIS Kubernetes benchmark with EKS clusters you\u2019re faced with false positive errors. With the CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark, you now have guidance aligned to the Amazon EKS cluster configuration and you should use this benchmark to assess and configure security for your cluster nodes. {"id": "77ee7302-1b23-4e37-8930-6144351ecc57", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "**Result: 5.4.1 passes and 5.4.2 fails.** This is based only on the three values you gave me. I didn't check the cluster itself.

| Control | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **5.4.1** Restrict access to the control plane endpoint | **Pass**, with a caveat | The public endpoint is on, but `publicAccessCidrs` is limited to `203.0.113.0/24`. It isn't the default `0.0.0.0/0`. |
| **5.4.2** Private endpoint enabled and public access disabled | **Fail** | `endpointPrivateAccess=true` meets the private half. `endpointPublicAccess=true` fails the "public access disabled" half. The CIDR restriction doesn't change this, because the control asks for the public endpoint to be off. |

**Caveats**
- **5.4.1:** `203.0.113.0/24` is the RFC 5737 documentation range (TEST-NET-3). It isn't routable on the internet. If you substituted a placeholder, re-run the check with the real CIDRs. If it's the real value, nobody can reach the public endpoint, so the setting is harmless but probably a misconfiguration. The pass also assumes the real range belongs to trusted egress IPs, such as your office or VPN.
- **Control wording:** The documentation search didn't return the benchmark text. I took the control titles and numbers from my knowledge of the CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark, section 5.4 (Cluster Networking). Section numbering can change between benchmark versions. Please confirm they match the version you're auditing against.

**Framework rows**
I can't tell you which framework rows these feed. I don't have your framework mapping, and I didn't want to guess row IDs. One verified cross-reference is the AWS Control Tower control CT.EKS.PR.1. It requires public access to the Kubernetes API endpoint to be disabled, so it lines up with 5.4.2 and would also fail. If you tell me which framework you mean (for example a specific compliance spreadsheet, Security Hub standard, or Control Tower), I can map the results to it.

**Remediation for 5.4.2**
To make 5.4.2 pass, turn off the public endpoint. Private access is already on, which is required first. Before you do, confirm that CI/CD, `kubectl` users and any other API clients can reach the private endpoint, for example through VPN, Direct Connect, a bastion host or a peered VPC. Once the public endpoint is off, `publicAccessCidrs` no longer has any effect. I can make that change with your approval if you want it, but I'd confirm connectivity first.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
